analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to disclose how they limit mental health coverage and allows audits of compliance.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and never received a vote or a hearing-reported action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would build on the existing mental health parity law, which requires insurance plans to cover mental health and substance use treatment no more restrictively than physical health care. It would force group health plans and insurers to publish each year the analyses they perform to prove they are complying with parity rules, especially on limits that are hard to quantify, like prior-authorization requirements. It would also direct three federal departments to run random audits of plans and collect data comparing how often mental health claims are denied versus other medical claims, and it would create a consumer unit at HHS with a toll-free number and website for people to file and track parity complaints.
analysis.who_benefits: People who need mental health or substance use treatment and their families: they would get access to the internal documents behind coverage decisions, a single place to file complaints, and published data on denial rates. Health care providers and patient advocacy groups would also gain from the added transparency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People needing mental health or addiction treatment

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to publish annual reports detailing the analyses they use to justify nonquantitative treatment limits — such as prior authorization and medical-necessity rules — on mental health and substance use benefits, including the factors, evidence standards, and conclusions for each service category [S3].

Requires the Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and the Treasury to run randomized audits of plans (no fewer than 12 per plan year) and to collect and report to Congress data comparing denial rates and reasons for mental health and substance use claims versus medical and surgical claims [S3].

Creates a consumer parity unit at HHS with a single toll-free number and a public website portal for filing and tracking parity complaints, and requires plans to timely respond to consumers' requests for information about their coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans would bear the cost of producing annual disclosure reports, responding to audits, and meeting complaint-response requirements. Some of those compliance costs could be passed to premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers with group plans

drawbacks.text: The audit floor is small — the bill requires audits of no fewer than 12 plans or coverages per plan year, a fraction of the plans subject to parity rules, so enforcement would depend heavily on the additional audit discretion it grants [S3].

Disclosure and audits do not by themselves change coverage; plans could document compliance rather than actually loosen restrictive practices, and the bill leaves enforcement outcomes to the departments' follow-through [S3].

Plans and issuers would face new reporting, recordkeeping, and complaint-response obligations under three separate statutes (PHSA, ERISA, and the tax code), costs that employers and insurers would bear and could pass into premiums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill asks for transparency — published analyses, denial-rate data, and a complaint channel — rather than rewriting benefit rules, so its direct cost to plans is compliance paperwork while its value to patients is real leverage to challenge unequal mental health coverage. Its main design weakness is thin mandatory audit volume and reliance on regulators to act on what disclosure reveals.

outcome.mechanism: It sat at the subcommittee level of three House committees — Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee, and later Education and the Workforce's Health subcommittee — and no committee ever reported it or scheduled a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 11, 2018 by Rep. Joseph Kennedy III with 8 original cosponsors, all Democrats; 9 Democratic cosponsors are recorded overall [S3][S4].

It was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — and was then referred to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce, the Health Subcommittee of Education and the Workforce, and the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee; the record shows no markup, no report, and no floor action [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2019 without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that fund group plans are better off because the bill died: they never had to publish the internal analyses behind their mental health coverage limits or face the new audit and complaint-response requirements. Patients seeking parity enforcement remain in the same position as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employers with group plans

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, but every recorded sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat, and the record shows no Republican support [S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill would require insurers to publish annually the analyses justifying hard-to-quantify limits on mental health benefits, face random audits, report denial-rate comparisons, and respond to consumer complaints. Insurers' existing practice — applying stricter limits to mental health care with little external scrutiny — is exactly what the bill's disclosure targets, so its compliance burden is the flip side of patients' leverage.

Employer group plans would be covered by the disclosure, audit, and complaint-response requirements under ERISA and the tax code provisions. Some employers already meet parity in practice and would mainly shoulder paperwork, while those relying on restrictive mental health management would face greater exposure.
